culture_note: Hip-hop is the mother tongue of half this community. This matrix is for the brothers who already carry hip-hop's rigor — pattern recognition, competitive craft, economy of language — and are moving it into code.
title: Hip-Hop Engineers
tagline: The culture already taught you the discipline. These men moved it into tech.

entries.name: Tim Burners Lee
entries.self_note: Not a Black man — included on this matrix only as the founder whose invention made every entry on this page possible. Every matrix names its foundation stone.
entries.claim: Invented the World Wide Web in 1989 at CERN, gave it away for free instead of patenting it, and still fights for an open web from the Web Foundation he founded.
entries.receipts: The first website (info.cern.ch, 1991) is still online. He could have patented the web — CERN released it into the public domain in 1993 on his push, and he has spent 30 years since keeping it un-patented and open. That's why your free GitHub Pages site costs $0 to run — the foundation is public.
entries.the_transfer: He gave away a trillion-dollar invention and never became a trillionaire. FED-EDU is built on the same open-source spirit — this whole repo is MIT-licensed free for any brother to copy, learn, and build on. When you get good, remember who paid for your ladder: pass it on. Open the ladder behind you.

entries.name: Mark Dean
entries.claim: The IBM engineer who co-invented the ISA bus — the architecture that let your keyboard, monitor, and disk talk to the PC — and later led the team that built the first gigahertz chip.
entries.receipts: Three of the original nine IBM PC patents have his name on them. He holds 20+ patents total. First Black IBM Fellow — the company's highest technical honor. Later became VP of the IBM research division at Almaden. He has said the thing he is proudest of is the team he built and the people he mentored — not the patents.
entries.the_transfer: Your entire dev rig exists because Mark Dean wired the parts to talk to each other. That is EXACTLY what we do in this repo — every blueprint's JS file bridges the UI to data with the same architecture thinking. He also spent his career mentoring: the FED-EDU version is the DAP and the pinned welcome threads. Build the bus. Then teach others to ride it.

entries.name: Clarence 'Software' Ellis
entries.claim: First Black American to earn a PhD in computer science (University of Illinois, 1969) — from a kid who got his first job guarding the office equipment at night and taught himself to use it.
entries.receipts: PhD 1969, then Bell Labs, then the Xerox PARC team that invented operational transformation — the technology inside Google Docs, Figma, and every real-time editor you've ever used. He also led the CSCW research field (Computer-Supported Cooperative Work — how people work together through software). Founder of the Black Data Processing Associates (BDPA) university chapters program.
entries.the_transfer: Ellis's OT research is why your FED-comm-DM and any collaborative editor works: multiple people typing without overwriting each other. More important is the path: night guard → self-taught → doctorate. The brother who only has access to a computer after hours — library terminal, night shift — has a PROVEN path in Ellis. The door was never fully closed. He found the gap and walked through.

entries.name: Dre's workstation
entries.self_note: This is the tools-become-the-craft entry. No man's name on it — the workstation itself is the story. It belongs because the Rig is the Rig.
entries.claim: Not a man — the workstation itself. The story of Dr. Dre's studio evolution from an SP-1200 sampler in a rented room to the digital rig that produced two of the highest-selling hip-hop albums ever, chronicled in the industry as the shift from hardware to software.
entries.receipts: The Chronic (1992) on the SP-1200 and live instruments — built on 12 seconds of sampled time. 2001 (1999) on Pro Tools and a wall of keyboards — built on unlimited digital time. Same producer, same ears, different rig. The Rig is the Rig: the craft transfers across hardware generations.
entries.the_transfer: Dre switched rigs mid-career and still made classics on both. The Rig is the Rig is a core FED-EDU teaching from the very first README: your 2015 Android on EasyTether can ship the same code as a $3000 tower — different rig, same craft. When you upgrade from the phone to the refurb PC (raffle), your skills transfer, you don't start over. Tools change. Ears stay.

entries.name: Chance the Rapper
entries.claim: The artist who proved you can reach the top of the music industry without signing away your masters — three Grammys for a FREE mixtape with no label.
entries.receipts: Coloring Book (2016): the first streaming-only album to win a Grammy (Best Rap Album, three Grammys total that night) — released FREE, label-free, via Apple Music streaming deal. He kept ownership of everything. His tour grossed $M; his merchandise is his own line; he closed the deal with Apple without giving up the masters. Then he turned around and donated $1 million to Chicago Public Schools.
entries.the_transfer: Chance kept his masters by refusing the label advance. That's the exact math of the FED-entry hustle: the 'advance' is the job offer that locks you in at a low rate forever. The free path — building your own platform, your own repo, your own clients — takes longer but you own everything you make. Read Coloring Book's business model before you sign anything.
